A0110.title: Firmware Secure Boot Mechanism
A0110.definition: A security mechanism that ensures a device only runs trusted, untampered firmware through cryptographic signature verification.
A0110.description: Secure Boot verifies firmware integrity during device startup to prevent loading of tampered or malicious firmware. Implementation steps include: storing a hardware Root of Trust key; signing firmware images with the manufacturer's private key; verifying signatures with the public key at boot time and denying boot if verification fails; employing a layered verification approach where each stage validates the next (UEFI Secure Boot model); and using a hardware Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to store integrity measurements. This mechanism is widely deployed in critical devices such as servers, IoT devices, and routers to ensure an unbroken chain of trust from hardware to the operating system.
A0110.limitation: Requires hardware support (TPM or equivalent chip), increasing costs; key management is complex, as a private key compromise exposes the entire device series to risk; prevents users from installing custom firmware, limiting openness; implementation errors may render devices inoperable (bricking).

A0110-001.title: XR Device Trusted Boot
A0110-001.description: XR headsets and companion devices implement firmware signature verification and secure boot mechanisms. Based on a hardware root of trust, they verify the signatures of firmware images layer by layer—including bootloader, operating system, and drivers. If signature verification fails, the boot process is refused, preventing malicious firmware from being implanted to hijack sensor data or the rendering layer for spatial computing attacks.

A0110-001.definition: Implement firmware signature verification and secure boot in XR devices to prevent malicious firmware.
A0110-001.limitation: Relies on the vendor's private key custody; if the private key is leaked, an attacker can sign arbitrary malicious firmware to bypass boot verification. Developer modes that unlock the bootloader and exploits (e.g., bootrom vulnerabilities) can break the chain of trust. Damage to or implementation errors in the hardware root of trust may brick the device, impacting normal users. Prevents users from installing custom firmware, which is unfriendly to researchers and power users, creating a conflict with openness demands.
